transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Hi, doctor. Thank you. Well... I guess what finally made me come in is that my appetite has just been all over the place for months. There are these long stretches where I just skip dinner entirely, and I've been losing weight without even trying. 

Which, honestly, my sister would probably kill for. She's been doing that strict keto thing since last Thanksgiving. I tried telling her—because, you know, being a healthcare social worker, I see people mess up their kidneys and cholesterol with fad diets all the time—but you know how sisters are, they never actually listen to you. She just bought this massive air fryer that takes up her entire kitchen counter, and she's always sending me pictures of pork rinds. 

But anyway... where was I? Oh, right, my appetite. So yeah, I'm losing weight, and on the nights I don't skip dinner, I just end up standing in the kitchen picking at saltine crackers or dry cereal. Cooking for myself just feels completely pointless lately. It's just too much effort.
Have you been feeling down or losing interest in things you usually enjoy, like hobbies or time with friends?

Well, I wouldn't say I'm feeling down all the time, exactly. But... I guess I just don't get the same spark from things anymore. Like, I still go through the motions with my garden. I'll go out and water the tomatoes, but it just feels so flat. I used to love being out there, getting my hands dirty. Which reminds me, I need to get a new pair of gardening gloves because the ones I have are completely worn through on the thumbs. I bought them at this little hardware store down the street, the one that's been there forever, you know? They have the creakiest wooden floors. But anyway, yeah, the garden just feels like a chore now. And my book club... I still show up, but I usually haven't even finished the book, or I just don't feel like talking, so I end up leaving early. Or sometimes I just can't even bring myself to start the book at all. It's just... I don't know, it's like the color is turned down on everything.
Have you been feeling unusually tired or like you don’t have much energy lately?

Yeah, I have. It's... it's honestly been a struggle just to get through the day. Even on days when my caseload at the hospital isn't unusually heavy, I just feel like I'm physically dragging my body down the hallways. The floors in the west wing are so hard, too—they just put in this new linoleum that's supposed to look like hardwood, but it's terrible on your joints. I keep telling the administration they need to invest in anti-fatigue mats for the nurses' stations, but you know how budgets are right now. They just cut funding for our art therapy program, which is a real shame because the patients really responded to it. 

But anyway, yeah, I'm just so exhausted. By the time I get home, I'm too tired to even think about cooking—which goes back to the saltines, I guess. I'm too tired to do my evening stretches, and I don't even have the energy to text people back. My phone just sits there buzzing with personal messages and I just... I can't even look at it.
Have you experienced days where you feel down or sad most of the time, not just a few hours here or there?

Well, I don't know if I'd say I feel sad most of the time. It's not like I'm sitting around crying all day or anything like that. I mean, my job is emotionally draining enough, you know? Just last week, we had this family come in, and they were arguing so loudly in the waiting room about their mother's discharge plan that security had to come over. It's always the siblings who live out of state who swoop in at the last minute and want to change everything the local caregiver has set up. I see it all the time. They feel guilty, so they overcompensate by demanding these completely unrealistic care plans. 

And then the paperwork... don't even get me started on the new electronic health record system they just forced us to switch to. They promised it would streamline everything, but it takes me ten clicks just to enter a single progress note now. My friend Sarah—she's a physical therapist on the fourth floor—she actually threatened to retire early because she hates the new system so much. 

But, um, what were you asking? Oh, feeling down. Yeah, I don't really think I feel sad all day long. It's more just... that tiredness and the flat feeling I mentioned before. Not really sadness, per se.
How long have you been feeling this way overall — the loss of appetite, the lack of interest in things, and the fatigue?

Well, I guess... it's been going on since the divorce was finalized. That was about a year and seven months ago. God, that whole process was just endless. His lawyer was incredibly unorganized. Every time we had a mediation session, they'd forget some crucial piece of financial disclosure. It honestly reminded me of trying to get Medicare to approve a complex discharge plan at the hospital—you fax them the exact same forms three times and they still claim they never received them. 

I swear, I spend half my day on hold with insurance companies, just listening to that awful elevator music. They always play this one jazz loop that cuts off right in the middle of a saxophone solo. It drives me completely up the wall, especially when I have three patients waiting for placement in a skilled nursing facility and the families are calling my desk every ten minutes for an update. I always tell the newer social workers to just put the phone on speaker and do their charting while they wait, otherwise you'll lose your mind. 

But, um... what did you ask? Oh, right, how long. Yeah, about a year and seven months, roughly. Ever since the ink dried on those divorce papers.
Over the past year and a half, have you had days where you felt down or hopeless for most of the day, nearly every day, not just off and on?

Hopeless? No, I don't think I'd use that word. Not every day, anyway. I mean, the system is hopeless, sure. Try getting a subsidized housing voucher approved in this county right now. The waitlist is just atrocious. I had this one gentleman last month, a sweet older guy, a retired mechanic, and he lost his apartment because his building got bought out by one of those luxury condo developers. 

They put up that awful gray siding on everything now, have you noticed that? Every new building looks exactly the same, like a giant filing cabinet. My neighborhood used to have all these beautiful old brick walk-ups, and now it's just endless gray rectangles with these minimalist coffee shops on the ground floor that charge seven dollars for a latte. And they don't even take cash anymore! I went in to buy a bran muffin the other day and the barista looked at my five-dollar bill like I had just handed him an antique. It’s just ridiculous how fast everything is changing, and they expect everyone to just keep up with all these apps and QR codes just to buy a pastry. 

But... wait, you asked about me feeling hopeless, right? Yeah, no, I don't think I feel hopeless myself most of the time. Just... running on empty, like I said.
Over the past year and a half, have you had periods where most days you felt down or low in mood for most of the day, not just a few hours here and there, even if it wasn’t constant sadness?

Low in mood... well, if you want to talk about low moods, you should see the general morale in my department right now. It is just completely in the gutter. We had this new girl start a couple of months ago, fresh out of her master's program. She was so bright-eyed, you know, thought she was going to fix the whole broken system single-handedly. She lasted exactly three weeks before she put in her notice to go work at some boutique private practice in the suburbs. 

Honestly, I don't even blame her. The parking situation at the hospital alone is enough to break a person's spirit. They tore up the main employee lot to build the new cardiac pavilion, so now we have to park at this satellite lot three blocks away and take a shuttle bus in. And the shuttle driver, Gary, he insists on blasting sports talk radio at 6:45 in the morning. Who wants to hear grown men screaming about football draft picks before they've even had their coffee? I tried bringing a book to read on the ride, but the suspension on that bus is so terrible it just gives me motion sickness. I told HR about it, but of course, that went into the same black hole as all our other complaints.

But, um... sorry, I lost my train of thought. You were asking if I had periods of feeling low? Honestly, no, I haven't really noticed long stretches like that. Like I was trying to say earlier, it's really just that flat, drained feeling. I wouldn't call it feeling down or low, just... empty, I guess.
Have you found that you no longer enjoy things that used to give you pleasure, even activities you really liked before?

Well, I still go through the motions of things I used to love, like watering the garden or showing up to my Wednesday night book club. But most of the time it just feels... flat, you know? I usually end up leaving early or sometimes I don't even start the activity at all. 

Speaking of the book club, Brenda picked the most ridiculous historical fiction novel this month. It was set in the Tudor period, but the author clearly didn't do any research on the clothing. They kept mentioning zippers, and I'm sitting there thinking, zippers weren't even invented until the late 1800s! It completely ruined the immersion for me. I tried to bring it up during the discussion, but Brenda got all defensive because it was a Reese Witherspoon book club pick or something. 

People are just so obsessed with whatever celebrities tell them to read these days. It's like nobody can form an independent opinion anymore. Just like my sister, she bought this absurdly expensive blender just because some influencer on Instagram said it cured her bloating. It's just a motor with blades, for heaven's sake! 

Anyway... yeah, the garden and the book club. I just don't get that same spark from them anymore. I just feel like I'm checking boxes.
Have you had a period lasting at least two weeks where you felt down or in a low mood for most of the day, nearly every day?

Two weeks... you know, two weeks is exactly how long my sister stayed with me last month. Two whole weeks in my guest room. And she brought her goldendoodle, which, let me tell you, is not nearly as hypoallergenic as those breeders claim. I spent half the time just vacuuming my living room rug. I have this gorgeous vintage Persian rug I found at an estate sale a few years back. The woman running the sale had absolutely no idea what she had, she was just trying to clear out her great-aunt's house as fast as possible and move back to Florida. I practically stole it for what I paid. But you have to be so careful cleaning it, you can't just run a regular beater-bar vacuum over it or it pulls the wool fibers right out... 

Wait, what was the question? A two-week period of feeling down? Right, sorry. No, I haven't really had a two-week stretch like that. Like I was saying before, it's not really a low or sad mood for me. I don't feel down, just... running on empty.
Can you recall if there was ever a two-week period or longer where you felt down or in a low mood for most of the day, nearly every day, even if it wasn't constant sadness?

Two weeks... well, I mean, I just answered that, didn't I? Two weeks is a long time. It feels like two weeks is about how long it takes to get an appointment with anyone these days. I tried to get my car in for an oil change last Tuesday, and the mechanic told me he was booked solid until the 14th. The 14th! For an oil change! It's not like I'm asking them to rebuild the transmission. It's just draining the oil and putting a new filter on. I used to do it myself when I was in college, back when cars actually had room under the hood to fit a wrench. Now everything is covered in these plastic shields, and you need a specialized computer just to tell the car it has new oil. It's a complete racket, if you ask me. They just want to force you to take it to the dealership so they can charge you double.

But anyway, to answer your question again... no. I don't think I've had a two-week period of feeling down or sad. Like I said, it's just that drained, empty feeling. Not sadness.
Over the past year and a half, have you had a period lasting at least two weeks where you felt in a low mood for most of the day, nearly every day?

I know, I know, you're asking about the two weeks again. A year and a half is a long time to think back on, though. A year and a half ago... that would have been right around the time the hospital switched over to the new electronic health record system. What an absolute nightmare that was. They promised us it would streamline our workflow and make coordinating care so much easier. Ha! I'm a social worker, I need to write actual narrative notes about my patients' living situations, not just click a bunch of drop-down menus. 

They had these "super users" walking around in bright yellow vests, supposedly there to help us if we got stuck. But half of them were just IT kids who had never spoken to a patient in their lives. I asked one of them how to document a complex family meeting regarding hospice placement, and he just stared at me and told me to put it in the "miscellaneous comments" box. The miscellaneous box! For an end-of-life care plan! It's just so dehumanizing, trying to reduce people's entire lives into these little sterile data fields. 

But, right, the two weeks of feeling low over the past year and a half. Honestly, Doctor, I feel like a broken record here, but no. I haven't had that. I really don't feel sad or low. It's just the emptiness, like I mentioned. Just... going through the motions.
Can you think back over the past year and a half and tell me if there was ever a time when you felt in a low mood most of the day, nearly every day, for at least two weeks straight?

You're asking me the exact same thing again. A year and a half, two weeks, low mood... I feel like we're just going in circles here. Circles... you know, that reminds me of this roundabout they just put in near my house. It used to be a perfectly fine four-way stop. Everyone knew exactly how it worked. You pull up, you wait your turn, you go. Simple. 

But no, the city council decided they needed to "improve traffic flow," so they spent six months tearing up the intersection to put in this massive roundabout. And nobody around here knows how to use it! People just stop dead right in the middle of the circle to let someone else in, which completely defeats the purpose. I was behind this guy in a silver Honda yesterday who yielded to a pedestrian who was still on the sidewalk, nowhere near the crosswalk. I laid on my horn, and he actually flipped me off! Can you believe that? 

I swear, the city planners just sit in their offices looking at blueprints and never actually drive on the roads they design. Just like those IT kids with the medical records system. 

Anyway... no. I'm sorry, I know you're just doing your job, but my answer is still the same. No two weeks of feeling sad or low. Just... empty.
Can you think back over the past year and a half and tell me if there was ever a time when you felt in a low mood most of the day, nearly every day, for at least two weeks straight?

Look, doctor, I... I really don't know how else to say it. You're asking the exact same question for the fourth time. A year and a half, two weeks, low mood. It's like... it's like when my sister calls me. She does this exact same thing. She'll call and ask if I'm coming to Sunday dinner, and I'll say no, I have to work. And then ten minutes later, she'll say, "So what time are you coming over on Sunday?" 

It drives me absolutely up the wall. She's been doing it since we were kids. Mom used to say she just had a "selective memory," but I think she just doesn't listen. Like last Thanksgiving, I told her three times I was bringing the sweet potatoes, and what does she do? She makes a massive batch of sweet potatoes herself, and then acts surprised when I walk in with mine. So we had two giant pans of sweet potatoes, and nobody even ate them because everyone was full from the turkey. 

I ended up taking mine to the nurses' station on Monday, and they devoured it in about five minutes. Nurses will eat anything you put in front of them, I swear. Especially if it has marshmallows on top. 

But... yeah. I'm sorry. I know I'm rambling. It's just frustrating being asked the same thing over and over. I haven't had a two-week period of feeling sad or low. I really haven't. It's just that drained feeling.
Over the past year and a half, have you had a period lasting at least two weeks where you felt in a low mood for most of the day, nearly every day?

Doctor, I... I feel like I'm losing my mind here. Are you... are you testing my patience? Because this is the fifth time you've asked me that exact same thing. It's like that movie, Groundhog Day. You know, with Bill Murray? Where he just wakes up and it's the exact same day, over and over again, with the same song playing on the radio. 

"I Got You Babe," right? Sonny and Cher. I actually saw Cher in concert once, years ago. Vegas. It was a girls' trip for my friend Linda's 40th birthday. Linda always had to do everything big. She insisted we all wear sequins, which, let me tell you, is not a comfortable fabric to sit in for three hours. And the drinks were outrageously expensive. I think I paid twenty dollars for a watered-down margarita. But Cher was incredible. She must have had fifteen costume changes. How does she even do that? She's older than I am and she's swinging around in a rhinestone leotard. 

I can't even get out of bed most days without my knees popping, let alone swing from the ceiling. Though, working at the hospital, I probably walk five miles a day just going between the different wards. 

But... look. To answer your question... again. No. I haven't been sad for two weeks straight. I haven't been low. I'm just empty. Drained. I don't know how else to explain it to you.

I tried bringing a book to read on the ride, but the suspension on that bus is so terrible it just gives me motion sickness. I told HR about it, but of course, that went into the same black hole as all our other complaints.

But, um... sorry, I lost my train of thought. You were asking if I had periods of feeling low? Honestly, no, I haven't really noticed long stretches like that. Like I was trying to say earlier, it's really just that flat, drained feeling. I wouldn't call it feeling down or low, just... empty, I guess.

patient.answer:
Well, I still go through the motions of things I used to love, like watering the garden or showing up to my Wednesday night book club. But most of the time it just feels... flat, you know? I usually end up leaving early or sometimes I don't even start the activity at all. 

Speaking of the book club, Brenda picked the most ridiculous historical fiction novel this month. It was set in the Tudor period, but the author clearly didn't do any research on the clothing. They kept mentioning zippers, and I'm sitting there thinking, zippers weren't even invented until the late 1800s! It completely ruined the immersion for me. I tried to bring it up during the discussion, but Brenda got all defensive because it was a Reese Witherspoon book club pick or something. 

People are just so obsessed with whatever celebrities tell them to read these days. It's like nobody can form an independent opinion anymore. Just like my sister, she bought this absurdly expensive blender just because some influencer on Instagram said it cured her bloating. It's just a motor with blades, for heaven's sake! 

Anyway... yeah, the garden and the book club. I just don't get that same spark from them anymore. I just feel like I'm checking boxes.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has experienced a depressed mood for most of the day, nearly every day, for at least a two-week period, which would support a diagnosis of Major Depressive Disorder (F32.9) over a persistent low mood seen in Persistent Depressive Disorder (F33.9).

patient.answer:
Two weeks... you know, two weeks is exactly how long my sister stayed with me last month. Two whole weeks in my guest room. And she brought her goldendoodle, which, let me tell you, is not nearly as hypoallergenic as those breeders claim. I spent half the time just vacuuming my living room rug. I have this gorgeous vintage Persian rug I found at an estate sale a few years back. The woman running the sale had absolutely no idea what she had, she was just trying to clear out her great-aunt's house as fast as possible and move back to Florida. I practically stole it for what I paid. But you have to be so careful cleaning it, you can't just run a regular beater-bar vacuum over it or it pulls the wool fibers right out... 

Wait, what was the question? A two-week period of feeling down? Right, sorry. No, I haven't really had a two-week stretch like that. Like I was saying before, it's not really a low or sad mood for me. I don't feel down, just... running on empty.

patient.answer:
Two weeks... well, I mean, I just answered that, didn't I? Two weeks is a long time. It feels like two weeks is about how long it takes to get an appointment with anyone these days. I tried to get my car in for an oil change last Tuesday, and the mechanic told me he was booked solid until the 14th. The 14th! For an oil change! It's not like I'm asking them to rebuild the transmission. It's just draining the oil and putting a new filter on. I used to do it myself when I was in college, back when cars actually had room under the hood to fit a wrench. Now everything is covered in these plastic shields, and you need a specialized computer just to tell the car it has new oil. It's a complete racket, if you ask me. They just want to force you to take it to the dealership so they can charge you double.

But anyway, to answer your question again... no. I don't think I've had a two-week period of feeling down or sad. Like I said, it's just that drained, empty feeling. Not sadness.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has experienced a persistently low mood for most of the day, nearly every day, for at least two weeks, to differentiate between F32.9 (Major Depressive Disorder, single episode) and F33.9 (Major Depressive Disorder, recurrent).

target_item.reason: The doctor is repeatedly asking about depressed/low mood (a core symptom of MDD), but my profile does not contain a specific symptom for Depressed Mood. I have already answered this question multiple times in the dialogue history.

patient.answer:
I know, I know, you're asking about the two weeks again. A year and a half is a long time to think back on, though. A year and a half ago... that would have been right around the time the hospital switched over to the new electronic health record system. What an absolute nightmare that was. They promised us it would streamline our workflow and make coordinating care so much easier. Ha! I'm a social worker, I need to write actual narrative notes about my patients' living situations, not just click a bunch of drop-down menus. 

They had these "super users" walking around in bright yellow vests, supposedly there to help us if we got stuck. But half of them were just IT kids who had never spoken to a patient in their lives. I asked one of them how to document a complex family meeting regarding hospice placement, and he just stared at me and told me to put it in the "miscellaneous comments" box. The miscellaneous box! For an end-of-life care plan! It's just so dehumanizing, trying to reduce people's entire lives into these little sterile data fields. 

But, right, the two weeks of feeling low over the past year and a half. Honestly, Doctor, I feel like a broken record here, but no. I haven't had that. I really don't feel sad or low. It's just the emptiness, like I mentioned. Just... going through the motions.

patient.answer:
You're asking me the exact same thing again. A year and a half, two weeks, low mood... I feel like we're just going in circles here. Circles... you know, that reminds me of this roundabout they just put in near my house. It used to be a perfectly fine four-way stop. Everyone knew exactly how it worked. You pull up, you wait your turn, you go. Simple. 

But no, the city council decided they needed to "improve traffic flow," so they spent six months tearing up the intersection to put in this massive roundabout. And nobody around here knows how to use it! People just stop dead right in the middle of the circle to let someone else in, which completely defeats the purpose. I was behind this guy in a silver Honda yesterday who yielded to a pedestrian who was still on the sidewalk, nowhere near the crosswalk. I laid on my horn, and he actually flipped me off! Can you believe that? 

I swear, the city planners just sit in their offices looking at blueprints and never actually drive on the roads they design. Just like those IT kids with the medical records system. 

Anyway... no. I'm sorry, I know you're just doing your job, but my answer is still the same. No two weeks of feeling sad or low. Just... empty.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has experienced a persistently low mood for most of the day, nearly every day, for at least two weeks, which is a key criterion for major depressive disorder (F32.9) versus persistent depressive disorder (F33.9).

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about depressed or low mood, which is not included in the patient's symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Look, doctor, I... I really don't know how else to say it. You're asking the exact same question for the fourth time. A year and a half, two weeks, low mood. It's like... it's like when my sister calls me. She does this exact same thing. She'll call and ask if I'm coming to Sunday dinner, and I'll say no, I have to work. And then ten minutes later, she'll say, "So what time are you coming over on Sunday?" 

It drives me absolutely up the wall. She's been doing it since we were kids. Mom used to say she just had a "selective memory," but I think she just doesn't listen. Like last Thanksgiving, I told her three times I was bringing the sweet potatoes, and what does she do? She makes a massive batch of sweet potatoes herself, and then acts surprised when I walk in with mine. So we had two giant pans of sweet potatoes, and nobody even ate them because everyone was full from the turkey. 

I ended up taking mine to the nurses' station on Monday, and they devoured it in about five minutes. Nurses will eat anything you put in front of them, I swear. Especially if it has marshmallows on top. 

But... yeah. I'm sorry. I know I'm rambling. It's just frustrating being asked the same thing over and over. I haven't had a two-week period of feeling sad or low. I really haven't. It's just that drained feeling.

patient.answer:
Doctor, I... I feel like I'm losing my mind here. Are you... are you testing my patience? Because this is the fifth time you've asked me that exact same thing. It's like that movie, Groundhog Day. You know, with Bill Murray? Where he just wakes up and it's the exact same day, over and over again, with the same song playing on the radio. 

"I Got You Babe," right? Sonny and Cher. I actually saw Cher in concert once, years ago. Vegas. It was a girls' trip for my friend Linda's 40th birthday. Linda always had to do everything big. She insisted we all wear sequins, which, let me tell you, is not a comfortable fabric to sit in for three hours. And the drinks were outrageously expensive. I think I paid twenty dollars for a watered-down margarita. But Cher was incredible. She must have had fifteen costume changes. How does she even do that? She's older than I am and she's swinging around in a rhinestone leotard. 

I can't even get out of bed most days without my knees popping, let alone swing from the ceiling. Though, working at the hospital, I probably walk five miles a day just going between the different wards. 

But... look. To answer your question... again. No. I haven't been sad for two weeks straight. I haven't been low. I'm just empty. Drained. I don't know how else to explain it to you.
